text:
COURT OF APPEAL FOR BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Yeoh v. Rawat,

2026 BCCA 114

Date: 20260309

Docket:
CA50941

Between:

Fayth
Hui Ching Yeoh

Appellant

(Plaintiff)

And

Sharnjit
Rawat and Manish Rawat

Respondents

(Defendants)

Before:

The Honourable Madam Justice Horsman

The Honourable Justice Gomery

The Honourable Justice Brundrett

On
appeal from:  An order of the Supreme Court of British Columbia, dated

August 26, 2025 (
Yeoh v. Rawat
,
2025 BCSC 1765
, Vancouver
Docket S254368).

Oral Reasons for Judgment

The Appellant, appearing in person:

F.H.C.
Yeoh

No one appearing on behalf of the
Respondents

Place and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver,
British Columbia

March
9, 2026

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
British Columbia

March
9, 2026

Summary:

The
appellant challenges an order striking her claim under Rule 9-5(1). Held:
Appeal allowed. The notice of civil claim could not be struck under any of the
subrules of R. 9-5(1). It presents an understandable claim for breach of
contract and of the
Business Practices and Consumer Protection Act
, it is not
frivolous or vexatious, there is nothing in the pleading that would prejudice,
embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing of the proceeding, and it is not
an abuse of process to pursue in the Supreme Court a claim that could be
advanced the Provincial Court or Civil Resolution Tribunal. The order
dismissing the action and requiring the appellant to pay costs is set aside.

GOMERY J.A.:

Overview

[
1
]

Ms. Yeoh contracted with Mr. Rawat and
Ms. Rawat to purchase from them a puppy for $800.  She was soon
dissatisfied with the dog and attempted to return it.  The Rawats refused to
take the dog back and return the $800.  Within a few days Ms. Yeoh
attended at the Rawats’ home with the dog and there was a confrontation which
ended after Ms. Yeoh called the police.  This was in February 2025.

[
2
]

In June 2025, Ms. Yeoh filed suit in the
Supreme Court of British Columbia.  In a notice of civil claim that was
evidently not drafted by a legal professional, she pleaded that she had been
promised a one‑month guarantee, that the dog was in good health, potty
trained outside and pee pad trained, and that the dog possessed a calm nature.
She pleaded that the Rawats had refused to honour their guarantee and that the
dog was incontinent and had various health issues.  She pleaded that the dog
had an aggressive nature and would terrorize her cat, her neighbours, and their
pets.  She claimed apparently substantial damages, invoking, among other
statutes, the
Sale of Goods Act
,

R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 410

and

the
Business Practices and Consumer Protection Act
,

S.B.C.
2004, c. 2.

[
3
]

The Rawats filed a handwritten response to civil
claim denying that they had given a warranty, asserting that the dog was
healthy, and denying responsibility for any costs incurred by Ms. Yeoh.

[
4
]

On August 5, 2025, the Rawats filed a notice of
application prepared by a lawyer seeking an order that the notice of civil
claim be struck in its entirety pursuant to
Supreme Court Civil Rule
9‑5(1)
as frivolous, vexatious and an abuse of process.  They sought special costs.  Ms. Yeoh
filed an application response expanding upon the facts and legal basis
underlying her claim.

[
5
]

The Rawats’ application came on for hearing
before a judge in chambers on August 26, 2025.  The parties were self‑represented.
The judge knew nothing about the case before it was called.  He was faced with
several binders of materials he had not had an opportunity to review.  After
hearing from the parties for a little less than an hour, he allowed the Rawats’
application and dismissed Ms. Yeoh’s action.  He gave oral reasons in a
single paragraph in which he stated that he had “never before seen a more
outrageous claim than this one”.  He described Ms. Yeoh’s claim as
misguided, devoid of merit, and one that could not possibly succeed.  He said:

It is plain and
obvious that this claim is scandalous, is vexatious, and is frivolous, and I am
not prepared to listen to you any longer -- … -- and I am striking this
plaintiff’s claim.

[
6
]

The chambers judge also ordered Ms. Yeoh to
pay lump sum costs of $3,000 to the Rawats.  The basis for this order, that is
whether the award reflects tariff costs or special costs, is unclear.

[
7
]

Ms. Yeoh appeals.  She is still self‑represented.
She has filed a factum.  The Rawats have not, and did not appear in court
today.  In a letter to the Court, they complain that Ms. Yeoh has not paid
the costs she was ordered to pay and ask for judgment in the amount of $1 million
for false arrest and damage to their reputation arising from the police
incident at their house.  The appeal record does not include a counterclaim or
a notice of cross appeal.

[
8
]

Both parties argued their positions before the
chambers judge as though on a summary trial, with their oral submissions
serving as evidence.  In her factum, Ms. Yeoh continues this approach on
appeal.  She accuses the Rawats of “misleading of court, contempt of court,
defamatory statements and multiple counts of perjury”.  She has applied to
adduce fresh evidence all of which would pertain to the merits of her claim
against the Rawats.

[
9
]

In my view, the judge was drawn into error by
the wide‑ranging arguments presented by the parties and an understandable
desire to bring an end to a lawsuit that appeared to him suitable for
resolution in the Small Claims Division of the Provincial Court or before the
Civil Resolution Tribunal in preference to the Supreme Court of British
Columbia.  The only issue properly before the judge was whether the notice of
civil claim should be struck.  The answer was that it should not.  The judge
ought to have dismissed the Rawats’ application.  I would allow the appeal.

Legal framework

[
10
]

A pleading is a document containing allegations
that have not yet been proved.  Rule 9‑5(1) authorizes the court to
strike a pleading or similar document and grant consequential relief.  The Rule
provides as follows:

Scandalous,
frivolous or vexatious matters

(1)   At any stage of a proceeding, the court may order
to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a pleading, petition or
other document on the ground that

(a)  it discloses no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may
be,

(b)  it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c)  it may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing
of the proceeding, or

(d)  it is otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court may pronounce judgment or
order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the application
to be paid as special costs.

[
11
]

An application under R. 9‑5(1) is not an application for
judgment on the merits based on proof of the facts alleged in a pleading.
Applications for summary judgment (R. 9‑6) or for judgment on a
summary trial (R. 9‑7) are different.  The focus under R. 9‑5
is on the character or quality of the pleading, not the quality of the
evidence.

[
12
]

Evidence is not admissible in relation to an attack on a pleading
under subrule (a) (fails to state a reasonable cause of action), but is
admissible in respect of the other subrules: R. 9‑5(2).

[
13
]

A pleading should only be struck under R. 9‑5(1) where,
assuming the facts pleaded to be true, it is plain and obvious that the attack
on it is well founded:
R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd.
,

2011
SCC 42
at para.
17
;
Willow v. Chong
,

2013 BCSC 1083

at para.
20
;
Nevsun Resources Ltd. v. Araya
,

2020 SCC 5

at paras.
64–66
.  In considering an application to strike, the pleading in
question is read generously and as a whole:
Lee v. G.Y Lee &
Associates Ltd.
,

2014 BCCA 400
at para.
14
.  Where the
pleading is functionally adequate, in that it provides an outline of material
allegations and the relief sought, minor defects may be overlooked if the
defendants are not prejudiced by them:
William v. British Columbia
,

2012
BCCA 285
at para.
106
, rev’d on other grounds,
2014 SCC 44
(as
Tsilhqot’in
Nation v. British Columbia
).

[
14
]

The judge described Ms. Yeoh’s claim as scandalous, frivolous,
and vexatious, invoking subrule (1)(b) of R. 9‑5.  A pleading
is vexatious or
frivolous
if it is
obvious
that it cannot succeed or give rise to a good
defence:
Skender v. Farley
,

2007 BCCA 629

at para.
64
;
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian
Jewish Congress
,

[1999] B.C.J. No. 2160,

1999 CanLII 5860
at para.
47
(S.C. Chambers)
[
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform
].  Under this subrule, the court may
have regard to extrinsic evidence of a history or circumstances said to make
the proceeding vexatious or frivolous, so that this category of attack may be
applied, for example, where the claim or defence is barred by the doctrines of
estoppel or
res judicata
:
Shoppers Drug Mart Inc. v. Mang
,
2021
BCSC 928
at para.
15
(Chambers).  A pleading is unnecessary or
scandalous if it pleads facts that are legally irrelevant to the substance of
the present dispute, so that it threatens to put the parties to the trouble and
expense of addressing collateral issues.  Such a pleading may also be
characterized as embarrassing or prejudicial to the fair trial of the
proceeding under subrule 1(c):
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform
,

para. 47;

Simon v Canada (Attorney General)
,
2017 BCSC 1438

at para.
52
, upheld
2018 BCCA 461
, citing
Sahyoun v. Ho
,

2015 BCSC 392
, aff'd
2017 BCCA 96
.

[
15
]

These various grounds of attack do not occupy watertight
silos.  They naturally overlap and a particular pleading may be subject to
attack on multiple grounds.

[
16
]

Ms. Yeoh’s fresh evidence application is governed by the
Palmer

test affirmed in
Barendregt v. Grebliunas
,

2022 SCC 22

at para.
29
.  It requires the Court to have regard to, among other
considerations, whether the evidence in question could reasonably have affected
the result in the court below.

Standard of review

[
17
]

Whether a pleading is susceptible to being struck under R. 9‑5(1)(a)
is a question of law.  This Court asks whether the decision was correct:
Situmorang
v. Google, LLC
,

2024 BCCA 9
at para.
52
. On the other
hand, the question of remedy is discretionary and is reviewed on a deferential
standard:
Situmorang

at para.
53
.

[
18
]

A decision to strike a pleading under one of the other subrules,
(b), (c) or (d) of R. 9‑5(1) is usually discretionary and the
standard of review is again deferential:
FORCOMP forestry Consulting Ltd. v.
British Columbia
,

2021 BCCA 465
, leave to appeal to SCC ref’d, 40051
(30 June 2022) at paras. 14–15.  The appellate court must consider whether
the decision involves a palpable and overriding error or may result in an
injustice, or if insufficient weight was given to relevant considerations.

The basis of the application to strike

[
19
]

Under “Legal Basis”, the Rawats’ notice of
application advanced the following arguments:

a)

The relief sought in the notice of civil claim was grossly
disproportionate to the nature of an $800 transaction to such an extent as to
be frivolous and vexatious;

b)

The sale of a dog is governed by the doctrine of
caveat emptor

and the defendants were under no obligation to disclose patent or obvious
defects;

c)

The notice of civil claim did not plead material facts to establish
false statements made negligently or fraudulently by the defendants, who denied
giving a guarantee or making representations; and

d)

The plaintiff’s excessive damages claim and sweeping allegations
were not grounded in law or fact and constituted a frivolous, vexatious and
abusive proceeding.

Analysis

[
20
]

The Rawats’ notice of application did not present a legally tenable
argument for an order striking the notice of civil claim.  Much of the argument
ignored the nature of the application as an attack on Ms. Yeoh’s
pleading.  Such an attack could not succeed on the basis that the defendants
denied giving a guarantee or making representations.  It could not succeed on
the basis that the defendants were under no obligation to disclose obvious
defects, because the notice of civil claim did not allege that Ms. Yeoh’s
complaint concerned obvious defects.

[
21
]

The notice of civil claim could not be struck under subrule (a)
of R. 9‑5(1).  While not a model, it presents an understandable
claim for breach of contract and breach of the
Business Practices and
Consumer Protection Act
.  Read generously, it is not obvious that the
notice of civil claim fails to state a reasonable cause of action.

[
22
]

The notice of civil claim could not be struck under subrule (b).
The claim stated is not frivolous or vexatious as those terms are understood in
the authorities.  It is not a claim that has been repeatedly advanced or is
being advanced in the teeth of a prior settlement.  Claiming excessive or even
disproportionate damages does not qualify.  The claim as a whole is not
scandalous.  It might be argued that it includes scandalous elements, but this
was not the argument advanced in the notice of application, and if it were so,
it could not justify striking the claim in its entirety and dismissing the
action.

[
23
]

The notice of civil claim could not be struck under subrule (c).
There is nothing in the pleading that would prejudice, embarrass or delay the
fair trial or hearing of the proceeding.

[
24
]

This leaves only the possibility that the claim might be viewed as
an abuse of the process of the court under subrule (d).  It is not an
abuse of process to pursue in the Supreme Court of British Columbia a claim
that could be advanced in the Provincial Court or before the Civil Resolution
Tribunal.  There is no lower bound to the Supreme Court’s monetary
jurisdiction.  Rule 14‑1(10) expressly addresses costs in respect of
claims brought within the Provincial Court’s monetary jurisdiction under the
Small
Claims Act
.

[
25
]

While deference is owed to the chambers judge’s decision, only
limited deference can be granted to reasons that are wholly conclusory.  There
was nothing on the face of the pleading to justify the judge’s description of
the claim as scandalous, frivolous, and vexatious, or any of them, and I can
only conclude that he misdirected himself as to the legal test to be applied.
He should not have struck the claim and dismissed Ms. Yeoh’s action on
this basis.

[
26
]

Ms. Yeoh’s application to adduce fresh evidence fails because,
to reiterate, the issue before the judge and on appeal is not whether her claim
against the Rawats should succeed at trial.  It is only whether the pleading
should be struck and the fresh evidence, or indeed any of the evidence Ms. Yeoh
would have us consider, does not bear on that question.

[
27
]

In light of my conclusion that the judge erred in allowing the
Rawats’ application and dismissing the action, the costs order against Ms. Yeoh
cannot stand.

Disposition

[
28
]

For these reasons, I would dismiss the fresh evidence application,
allow the appeal and set aside the orders of the chambers judge allowing the
application to strike, dismissing the action, and requiring the appellant to
pay costs.

[
29
]

Before the chambers judge, Ms. Yeoh had brought applications
for leave to amend her notice of civil claim.  The judge did not address these
applications and they are not before us.  Ms. Yeoh may pursue them in the
Supreme Court, as she may think fit.

[
30
]

HORSMAN J.A.
: I agree.

[
31
]

BRUNDRETT J.A.
: I agree.

[
32
]

HORSMAN J.A.
: The fresh evidence
application is dismissed. The appeal is allowed. This Court sets aside the
orders of the chambers judge allowing the application to strike, dismissing the
action, and requiring the appellant to pay costs.

“The Honourable Justice Gomery”
